```{r}
#| include: false
m1 <- glm(f_true, data = dev, family = binomial)
dev$risk <- predict(m1, type = "response")
```

## Where we are

::: {.incremental}
- Session 1: a model that gives a **risk** for each adult
- Today: **how good** are these risks? Two questions:
  - **Discrimination**: does the model **rank** adults with diabetes above those without?
  - **Calibration**: are the **risks themselves right**?
- (Both are still **apparent** here: in the development data)
:::

# Topic 1 — Discrimination {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## ROC curve and AUC

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 4.4
roc1 <- roc(dev$diabetes, dev$risk, quiet = TRUE)
plot(roc1, legacy.axes = TRUE, col = col_blue, lwd = 3, print.auc = TRUE)
```

```{r}
ci.auc(roc1)
```

::: {.key}
**AUC 0.80** (95% CI 0.75 to 0.85). It is the probability that a **randomly chosen adult with diabetes has a higher predicted risk** than one without. **0.5 = coin toss, 1 = perfect**. A common reading: 0.7 to 0.8 acceptable, 0.8 to 0.9 good, but the **usefulness depends on the use**.
:::

## A threshold

```{r}
tab <- table(predicted = dev$risk >= 0.15, diabetes = dev$diabetes); tab
round(c(sensitivity = tab["TRUE", "1"] / sum(tab[, "1"]), specificity = tab["FALSE", "0"] / sum(tab[, "0"]),
        PPV = tab["TRUE", "1"] / sum(tab["TRUE", ]), NPV = tab["FALSE", "0"] / sum(tab["FALSE", ])), 2)
```

::: {.incremental}
- At **15%**: sensitivity **0.62**, specificity **0.78**, PPV **0.28**, NPV **0.94**
- **Lower the threshold**: sensitivity **up**, specificity **down** (more adults tested)
- **PPV and NPV depend on the prevalence**: they change from district to district
- The **AUC** summarises **all thresholds**; the **choice of threshold** needs **costs and benefits** (Session 5)
:::

## Added value

```{r}
c(age_only = auc_of(dev$diabetes, predict(glm(diabetes ~ age, data = dev, family = binomial), type = "response")), full_model = auc_of(dev$diabetes, dev$risk)) |> round(3)
```

Age alone gives **0.68**; the full model **0.80**: the other predictors add **real discrimination**.

# Topic 2 — Calibration {background-color="#2C3E50"}

## Calibration plot

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
#| fig-height: 4.4
cal <- dev |> mutate(decile = ntile(risk, 10)) |> group_by(decile) |> summarise(predicted = mean(risk), observed = mean(diabetes))
ggplot(cal, aes(predicted, observed)) + geom_abline(linetype = 2) + geom_point(size = 3, colour = col_blue) + geom_line(colour = col_blue) + coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 0.6), ylim = c(0, 0.6)) + labs(x = "Mean predicted risk", y = "Observed proportion with diabetes")
```

::: {.key}
Group the adults by **deciles of predicted risk** and compare the **mean predicted** with the **observed** proportion. **Points on the diagonal** = well calibrated. **Below** = the model **over-estimates**; **above** = it **under-estimates**.
:::

## Calibration slope and intercept

```{r}
lp <- qlogis(dev$risk)
round(coef(glm(diabetes ~ lp, data = dev, family = binomial)), 3)
```

::: {.warn}
Intercept **0** and slope **1.000** in the development data: this is **guaranteed** when a logistic model is fitted by maximum likelihood. It says **nothing** about new patients. In **new data**: **slope below 1** = predictions **too extreme** (overfitting); **intercept (calibration-in-the-large)** shows **average over- or under-estimation**.
:::

## Brier score

```{r}
brier <- mean((dev$risk - dev$diabetes)^2); brier_null <- mean((mean(dev$diabetes) - dev$diabetes)^2)
round(c(brier = brier, scaled = 1 - brier / brier_null), 3)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **Brier** = mean squared difference between **risk and outcome** (0 = perfect); combines **discrimination and calibration**
- **Scaled Brier** = 1 − Brier / Brier of "everyone gets the prevalence": **0.15** here (0 = no better than the prevalence)
- Avoid the **Hosmer-Lemeshow test**: it depends on the grouping, has low power and says **nothing about how** the calibration fails
:::

## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p2q1", "How do you read an AUC of 0.80?",
         c("80% of the adults are classified correctly if a threshold of 50% is used",
           "The predicted risks are within 20% of the true risks, on average, for adults",
           "A random case has a higher risk than a random non-case, 80% of the time",
           "The model explains 80% of the variation in diabetes within the cohort studied"), answer = 3,
         explain = "The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen case has a higher predicted risk than a randomly chosen non-case. It says nothing about the calibration of the risks.")
```

## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p2q2", "A threshold of 15% gives a sensitivity of 0.62. What happens when the threshold is lowered to 5%?",
         c("Both sensitivity and specificity rise",
           "Sensitivity rises and specificity falls",
           "Sensitivity falls and specificity rises",
           "Neither changes, since the AUC does not depend on the threshold"), answer = 2,
         explain = "A lower threshold labels more adults as positive, so more cases are found (higher sensitivity) but more non-cases are labelled positive (lower specificity).")
```

## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p2q3", "In the development data the calibration slope is exactly 1 and the intercept 0. What does this tell you?",
         c("The model is well calibrated and will be well calibrated in other cohorts",
           "The model does not overfit, since the slope is not below 1 in these data",
           "Nothing about new patients: it is guaranteed by the fitting",
           "The predicted risks are accurate for each of the risk groups in the cohort"), answer = 3,
         explain = "Maximum likelihood forces the apparent calibration to be perfect. Calibration has to be assessed in new data or with a bootstrap.")
```

## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p2q4", "In a calibration plot the points lie below the diagonal at high predicted risk. What does that mean?",
         c("The model under-estimates risk, since more events are observed than predicted",
           "The model discriminates poorly, with an AUC close to 0.5",
           "The sample is too small to draw a calibration plot",
           "The model over-estimates risk: fewer events are observed than predicted"), answer = 4,
         explain = "Observed proportions below predicted ones mean that the predicted risk is too high. Discrimination is a separate question.")
```

## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
quiz_mcq("p2q5", "Why do PPV and NPV differ between a screening clinic and the general population for the same model?",
         c("They depend on the prevalence of the disease in the population",
           "The AUC of the model changes with the setting by definition",
           "Sensitivity and specificity are defined in clinics but not elsewhere",
           "The threshold has to be changed when the setting changes"), answer = 1,
         explain = "Predictive values combine sensitivity and specificity with the prevalence. With a higher prevalence, the PPV rises and the NPV falls.")
```

## Score and take-home

**Your score: <span class="quiz-score"></span>**

::: {.incremental}
- **Discrimination**: AUC = chance of ranking a case above a non-case
- **Threshold**: sensitivity, specificity; PPV/NPV depend on **prevalence**
- **Calibration**: plot, **slope** (spread), **intercept** (average level)
- Apparent slope is always **1**: check in **new data**
- **Brier** combines both; avoid Hosmer-Lemeshow
:::
